library(tidyverse)

# Problem 1
```{r}
data("ny_noaa")
```

```{r}
ny_noaa
```

```{r}
str(ny_noaa)
```
```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    missing_prcp = mean(is.na(prcp)),
    missing_snow = mean(is.na(snow)),
    missing_snwd = mean(is.na(snwd)),
    missing_tmax = mean(is.na(tmax)),
    missing_tmin = mean(is.na(tmin))
  )
```

The ny_noaa dataset has 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. It includes the station ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature. The date variable is stored as a date, precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth are stored as integers, and id, maximum, and minimum temperature are stored as character variables. There is a decent amount of missing data mostly for temperature, about 5.6% of precipitation values are missing, 14.7% of snowfall values are missing, 22.8% of snow depth values are missing, and about 43.7% of both maximum and minimum temperature values are missing.

```{r}
ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(
    date,
    into = c("year", "month", "day"),
    sep = "-"
  )
```

```{r}
ny_noaa
```

```{r}
ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
```

```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  count(snow) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

The most common snowfall value is 0 mm which makes sense because most days do not have any snowfall. The other common values are: 25, 13, 51, and 76 mm. These values probably occur often because snowfall was originally recorded in common inch amounts and then converted to millimeters.

```{r}
ny_noaa_monthly =
  ny_noaa |>
  filter(month == "01" | month == "07") |>
  drop_na(tmax) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year)
  ) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax)
  )
```

```{r}
ny_noaa_monthly |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, color = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (C)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

January temperatures vary a lot more across stations and years than July temperatures. Most January averages are around or below 0°C and July averages are mostly in the mid to upper 20s. There are also a few noticeable outliers, including some very cold January averages and a few low July averages.

```{r}
ggp_tmax_tmin =
  ny_noaa |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmax, y = tmin)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Maximum Temperature (C)",
    y = "Minimum Temperature (C)"
  )
```

```{r}
ggp_snow =
  ny_noaa |>
  filter(
    snow > 0,
    snow < 100
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = snow)) +
  geom_violin(aes(group = year)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1981, 1990, 2000, 2010)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  )
```

```{r}
ggp_tmax_tmin + ggp_snow
```

Maximum and minimum temperature have a strong positive relationship, with most observations concentrated on a diagonal pattern. There are also a few outlier temperature values. The snowfall distributions are pretty similar across years where most snowfall values below 100 mm concentrated at several common amounts and no major change in the overall distribution over time.

# Problem 2
```{r}
nhanes_covar_df =
  read_csv(
    "./data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4
  )
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_df
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_df =
  nhanes_covar_df |>
  janitor::clean_names()
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_df =
  nhanes_covar_df |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na()
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_df =
  nhanes_covar_df |>
  mutate(
    sex =
      case_match(
        sex,
        1 ~ "male",
        2 ~ "female"
      ),
    sex = as.factor(sex),
    education =
      case_match(
        education,
        1 ~ "Less than high school",
        2 ~ "High school equivalent",
        3 ~ "More than high school"
      ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )
```

```{r}
nhanes_accel_df =
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv")
```

```{r}
nhanes_accel_df
```

```{r}
nhanes_accel_df =
  nhanes_accel_df |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  )
```

```{r}
nhanes_accel_df =
  nhanes_accel_df |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  )
```

```{r}
nhanes_df =
  left_join(
    nhanes_covar_df,
    nhanes_accel_df,
    by = "seqn"
  )
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The number of men and women are similar in the less than high school and more than high school groups. The high school equivalent group has more men than women and the more than high school group has the largest number of participants overall.

```{r}
nhanes_covar_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex"
  )
```

The age distributions differ a little across education groups. The more than high school group has more younger participants mostly among women, and the less than high school and high school equivalent groups include more older participants. The male and female distributions overlap mostly overall, even though there are some differences within each education group.

```{r}
nhanes_total_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims)
  )
```

```{r}
nhanes_total_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total Activity",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Total activity generally decreases with age across all three education groups. The male and female trends overlap a lot even though there are some differences depending on education level and age. The decline with age is steep in the less than high school group and there is also one very low activity value or outlier in the more than high school group.

```{r}
nhanes_time_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

```{r, fig.width=9}
nhanes_time_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 360, 720, 1080),
    labels = c("12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", "6 PM")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity by Sex and Education",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Average MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Activity is lowest overnight, rises quickly in the morning, stays high during the day, and decreases again at night. Men and women follow a similar overall pattern across all education groups. Women have slightly higher daytime activity particularly in the high school equivalent and more than high school groups.

# Problem 3
```{r}
jan_2020_df =
  read_csv("./data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  )

jan_2024_df =
  read_csv("./data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  )

july_2020_df =
  read_csv("./data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  )

july_2024_df =
  read_csv("./data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  )
```

```{r}
citibike_df =
  bind_rows(
    jan_2020_df,
    jan_2024_df,
    july_2020_df,
    july_2024_df
  )
```

```{r}
citibike_df
```

The combined Citi Bike dataset has 99,485 rides and 9 variables. It includes information about the bike type, day of the week, ride duration, starting and ending stations, and whether the rider was a member or casual rider. I also added year and month variables so the rides from January and July of 2020 and 2024 can be compared.

```{r}
citibike_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Members took more rides than casual riders in every month and year shown. Ridership was also a lot higher in July than in January. Both member and casual ridership increased from 2020 to 2024 and the largest number of rides were in July 2024.

```{r}
citibike_df |>
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    month == "July"
  ) |>
  count(start_station_name) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(5) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers was the most popular starting station in July 2024, it had 163 rides, then University Pl & E 14 St with 155 rides.

```{r}
citibike_duration_df =
  citibike_df |>
  mutate(
    weekdays =
      case_match(
        weekdays,
        "Monday" ~ "Mon",
        "Tuesday" ~ "Tue",
        "Wednesday" ~ "Wed",
        "Thursday" ~ "Thu",
        "Friday" ~ "Fri",
        "Saturday" ~ "Sat",
        "Sunday" ~ "Sun"
      ),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu",
        "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"
      )
    ),
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration)
  )
```

```{r, fig.width=9}
citibike_duration_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = weekdays,
      y = median_duration,
      color = month
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(. ~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Day, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration",
    color = "Month"
  )
```

Median ride duration was higher in July than in January for every day of the week in both years. The ride durations were also generally higher in 2020 than in 2024. In 2020, weekend rides were longer in July. Also, the differences across days were smaller in 2024.

```{r, fig.width=9}
citibike_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = member_casual,
      y = duration,
      fill = member_casual
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin() +
  facet_grid(month ~ rideable_type) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration in 2024",
    x = "Rider Type",
    y = "Ride Duration",
    fill = "Rider Type"
  )
```

Casual riders had longer rides than members for both classic and electric bikes in January and July. Ride durations were also longer in July than in January, particularly for casual riders. For casual riders, classic bike rides seem to be longer than electric bike rides, and the member distributions were more similar across bike types. The distributions also have long upper tails which show that some rides lasted much longer than the typical ride.
